extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literature, and creative writers interested in narrative techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and produce narratives using the Russian skaz technique: an oral, stylized mode of narration that adopts a character's voice through dialect and slang and is integrated into the surrounding prose. Includes distinctions such as simple/objectified skaz versus double-voiced (parodic) skaz and guidance by historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dialect and slang to adopt a persona
rubrics_metrics.description: The speech makes use of dialect and slang in order to take on the persona of a particular character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion emphasizes that the narrator's voice should reflect specific regional, social, or colloquial speech patterns so the narrative voice itself embodies a character. Examples of practitioners include Leskov, Gogol, and later writers; such language choices signal the skaz technique rather than neutral authorial prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into surrounding narrative (not quoted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar speech... is integrated into the surrounding narrative, and not presented in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skaz blends the oral/colloquial speech directly into the narrative voice instead of isolating it as reported dialogue. Look for continuous narrative in which the colloquial register persists across exposition and commentary—an anti-pattern is treating the voice as isolated quoted talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral, unmediated or improvisational quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Skaz is a Russian oral form of narrative; Eikhenbaum described the phenomenon as a form of unmediated or improvisational speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narration should feel spontaneous, as if told aloud; sentence-level irregularities, digressions, hedging, and performative contingencies can reproduce an improvisatory oral feel. Avoid overly polished, uniformly 'literary' diction if aiming for authentic skaz effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as a literary device and performance element
rubrics_metrics.description: Skaz is not only a literary device, but is also used as an element in Russian monologue comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skaz can serve both aesthetic (stylization, characterization) and performative/comedic functions. When applying skaz, consider how the voice functions rhetorically—to satirize, amuse, or create intimacy with the listener/reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylization and voice distinction (simple vs double-voiced skaz)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bakhtin distinguishes between skaz as a simple form of objectified discourse (as found in Turgenev or Leskov), and double-voiced skaz, where an author's parodistic intention is evident (as found in Gogol or Dostoevsky).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the narrator's voice is presented straightforwardly (simple/objectified) or layered with authorial irony/parody (double-voiced). Double-voiced skaz requires signals that the author is manipulating the narrator's voice to critique or mock it; simple skaz preserves the voice as an autonomous discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and historical anchoring in oral tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Eikhenbaum saw skaz as central to Russian culture, and believed that a national literature could not develop without a strong attachment to oral traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or writing skaz, attend to its roots in oral storytelling—reliance on communal forms, folk patterns, and performative expectation. The device often invokes cultural memory and collective speech forms; the criterion matters more in culturally-inflected works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across literatures (identify analogous elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term is also used to describe elements in the literature of other countries; modern critics find examples in works like The Catcher in the Rye and Vernon God Little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skaz is not strictly limited to Russian-language texts; look for the same constellation of features—colloquial persona, integrated speech, oral/improvisational feel, and possible double-voicing—in other languages. Use cross-literary examples (Salinger, DBC Pierre, David Lodge's writings) as models for adaptation or comparative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author and practitioner exemplars as identification guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Nineteenth-century users: Nikolai Leskov and Pavel Melnikov (and Gogol). Twentieth-century practitioners include Mikhail Bulgakov, Aleksey Remizov, Mikhail Zoshchenko, Andrei Platonov, and Isaac Babel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use canonical examples to study technique: read listed authors to see how they realize skaz in practice. These exemplars illustrate the range from simple to double-voiced skaz and the device’s deployment in different genres and registers.
